claims.text: Premelting onset and progression in Fe-Ni-Cr-Co-Cu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles are governed by local chemical-ordering heterogeneity.
Regions enriched in lower-melting-point elements act as nucleation sites for premelting.
Segregated regions cause premelting to begin earlier than it does in particles with a uniform atomic distribution.
Chemical segregation broadens the melting transition relative to a more homogeneous particle.
The examined Fe-Ni-Cr-Co-Cu nanoparticles are initially solid and single phase.
Five-element nanoparticles can have a largely mixed or random elemental distribution while retaining local compositional fluctuations or segregation.
Laser ablation can produce nominally uniform Fe-Ni-Cr-Co-Cu nanoparticles with inherent nanoscale compositional fluctuations.
Controlled processing changes or post-synthesis annealing can be used to enhance local compositional segregation in these nanoparticles.
Limited atomic mobility influences whether multielement nanoparticles remain randomly mixed or develop preferred local structures.
Increasing the local concentration of lower-melting-point constituents reduces the local effective melting temperature.
Spatial compositional heterogeneity creates a distribution of local melting temperatures across a nanoparticle.
A distribution of local melting temperatures produces a broader overall melting transition.
Engineered segregated particles will have a lower premelting-onset temperature than homogeneous baseline particles.
Engineered segregated particles will have a wider melting transition than homogeneous baseline particles.
Particles with a uniform elemental distribution will exhibit a sharper transition at a higher and more uniform temperature.
Surface and interface effects are significant for particles with sizes on the order of a few nanometers.
The proposed mechanism is limited to conditions in which atomic mobility remains restricted during high-temperature processing.
The mechanism may not apply to bulk materials or when thermal diffusion substantially homogenizes the local composition.
Surface effects and kinetic limitations during rapid heating or cooling may influence the observed melting response.
A lack of a statistically significant difference in premelting onset or transition width between homogeneous and segregated particles would falsify the proposed governing mechanism.
